chapters.title: Chapter 4: Deep Learning Foundations for Market Sequences

lessons.title: Case Study: An LSTM Volatility Forecaster for Nifty Bank

body.text: This case study is the whole course in miniature: a genuine deep learning model, built with real discipline, walk-forward tested not just against a cheaper CNN baseline but against a 40-year-old classical benchmark that has quietly outperformed a great deal of fancier machinery for decades. If the LSTM cannot clear that bar, no amount of architecture sophistication makes it worth deploying.

children.text: The Problem: Forecasting Next-Day Realized Volatility on Nifty Bank

This case study forecasts a continuous number, next-day realized volatility on Nifty Bank, a regression problem, not the classification problems built so far. The input is a windowed sequence of trailing daily returns, absolute returns, and squared returns, normalized within each window per the previous lesson's rule. The task suits an LSTM's evolving memory specifically because of volatility clustering, the well-documented tendency, going back to Mandelbrot's 1963 observation and formalized in Engle's 1982 ARCH model, for large price moves to be followed by more large moves, calm periods by more calm. A model that carries forward a sense of how turbulent recent days have been is working with the grain of that structure, not against it.
The Baseline You Must Beat: GARCH(1,1)

markDefs.definition: Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity, a family of classical volatility models introduced by Engle (1982) and generalized by Bollerslev (1986). GARCH(1,1) forecasts tomorrow's variance as a weighted combination of a long-run average, yesterday's squared return, and yesterday's forecast variance.

children.text: Before any neural network gets built, there is a decades-old, industry-standard model that must be walk-forward tested first:

. It is simple, robust, and, precisely because it encodes volatility clustering directly into its structure, genuinely difficult to beat. Any LSTM built for this problem inherits the same obligation every model in this course has faced: prove it clears a real baseline, not just that it produces plausible-looking forecasts in isolation.

body.caption: Tomorrow's forecast variance is a weighted blend of a long-run average level (ω), yesterday's squared return (α, reacting to the latest shock), and yesterday's own forecast variance (β, persistence). With α + β close to but below 1, shocks decay slowly, exactly the clustering behavior this lesson's LSTM is also trying to capture.

children.text: The architecture is the previous lesson's LSTM with two changes: no sigmoid on the output, since this is a continuous forecast, not a probability, and mean squared error as the loss instead of binary cross-entropy. Everything else, small hidden size, dropout, weight decay, gradient clipping, chronological early stopping, carries over unchanged.

body.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class LSTMVolForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size=16, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, batch_first=True)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        _, (h_n, _) = self.lstm(x)
        out = self.drop(h_n[-1])
        return self.fc(out).squeeze(-1)   # no sigmoid: a volatility forecast, not a probability

model = LSTMVolForecaster(input_size=3)  # daily return, |return|, squared return
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
body.caption: Three input channels per day, return, absolute return, and squared return, deliberately mirror the terms GARCH itself uses, giving the LSTM the same raw information as its classical competitor rather than a completely different feature set.

body.text: These figures are an illustrative worked example built to show how a deep learning model should be benchmarked against both a cheaper ML alternative and a classical baseline, not a live or historical track record for any specific fund or model.

This is the third case study in this course, and the third time the same shape has appeared: the more sophisticated model's edge is small in calm years and concentrated in the volatile or regime-transition ones, 2020's COVID spike and 2022's choppiness here, exactly the pattern seen in Chapter 2's momentum signal and Chapter 3's Bank Nifty rotation. GARCH's slow, backward-looking persistence term adapts gradually to a sudden regime change; the LSTM's more flexible memory can pick up the shift faster, which is precisely where its added complexity earns its keep.

children.text: What the LSTM Learned (and a SHAP-Equivalent Sanity Check)

Chapter 2 made TreeSHAP a non-negotiable step for every tree ensemble in this course. A neural network needs the equivalent scrutiny, not a pass. TreeSHAP itself does not apply to an LSTM, but shap.DeepExplainer, part of the same SHAP library, and Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan, 2017) both attribute a neural network's output back to its inputs using methods suited to differentiable models. Running either against this LSTM's inputs, return, absolute return, and squared return, at each position in the window, is how you would check whether the model is actually leaning on the terms GARCH itself trusts, or drifting toward something less defensible.

body.text: Being a neural network does not exempt a model from this course's interpretability standard. It changes which tool you reach for, DeepExplainer or Integrated Gradients instead of TreeSHAP, not whether you reach for one at all.

children.text: The LSTM beats GARCH(1,1) modestly on average and meaningfully in volatile years, and the CNN captures most, though not all, of that same edge at a fraction of the training cost, echoing the previous lesson's advice to try the cheaper option first. Rather than choosing exactly one of the three, the most defensible next step is the one Chapter 3 already built the machinery for: a small stacked ensemble with GARCH, the CNN, and the LSTM as base forecasts and a simple linear meta-learner deciding how much to trust each one, likely leaning on GARCH in calm periods and the LSTM specifically when its own out-of-fold behavior signals a regime shift is underway.

This closes the four chapters built so far: why trading ML is different, tree-based ensembles, stacking, and deep learning on sequences, sharing one continuous set of habits, correct labeling, honest validation, active leak-checking, and interpretability, applied to four genuinely different model families. Further chapters, if added later, would be a natural place for attention and transformer architectures for longer sequences, a deeper look at validating deep learning models specifically, and the practical work of moving a model like this one from a notebook into production.

body.title: Volatility Forecasting Production Checklist
steps: GARCH(1,1), or a comparable classical baseline, walk-forward tested first, so you know the exact number any ML model needs to beat
LSTM and CNN forecasters both built and compared, not just the model you started with
Every window normalized using only its own trailing statistics, never a global training-set statistic
Improvement over GARCH checked fold by fold across regimes, not just as a single averaged number
A DeepExplainer or Integrated Gradients pass run on the LSTM, so it is not the one model in this course left unexamined
A hybrid, GARCH blended with the ML forecast through a stacked meta-learner, considered as seriously as either model alone, especially if ML's edge is concentrated in a few volatile folds

body.title: Why GARCH Is the Right Baseline Here
body.textWithBlank: Before trusting an LSTM's volatility forecast, it must be walk-forward compared against GARCH(1,1), a decades-old, industry-standard model, because a sophisticated model that cannot beat a simple, well-established ___ has not actually earned its added complexity.
body.explanation: This is the same discipline Chapter 3 applied when it insisted a stacked ensemble be compared against its own best single base model, not judged in isolation. An LSTM volatility forecaster has no more right to skip that comparison than any tree ensemble did, and GARCH(1,1), despite being decades old, remains a genuinely difficult baseline to beat in calm markets.

points: Volatility clustering, the tendency for large moves to follow large moves, is why this case study is a regression problem well suited to an LSTM's evolving memory, unlike the classification problems built earlier in this course
GARCH(1,1) is the required baseline for any volatility forecasting model; it encodes clustering directly into a simple, decades-old formula that remains genuinely hard to beat

This case study's LSTM improved on GARCH by an average of about 0.32 RMSE points, concentrated in the volatile 2020 and choppy 2022 folds, echoing the same regime-dependent pattern seen in Chapters 2 and 3's case studies
A CNN baseline captured most of the LSTM's edge at lower training cost, confirming the previous lesson's advice to try the cheaper model first
shap.DeepExplainer and Integrated Gradients are the neural-network equivalents of TreeSHAP; being a deep learning model does not exempt it from this course's interpretability standard
The most defensible next step is not choosing one model, it is stacking GARCH, the CNN, and the LSTM together with a linear meta-learner, using Chapter 3's own machinery to combine them
